items.prompt: The DASH-Sodium trial tested a healthy eating pattern at different salt levels in 412 people. How did the researchers control what participants ate?

options.A: They gave participants recipes and shopping lists, then checked progress monthly
options.B: They asked participants to keep detailed food diaries and estimated sodium from them
options.C: They supplied participants' meals, with each salt level eaten for 30 days
options.D: They delivered groceries to participants' homes and added dietitian counselling

items.prompt: A trial of about 21,000 people in rural China tested whether a potassium-enriched salt substitute prevents strokes. How was it designed?

options.A: 600 villages were randomly assigned to the substitute or regular salt, and strokes and deaths were counted over about five years
options.B: People who had chosen the substitute were compared with people who had chosen regular salt, and their stroke rates were tracked
options.C: Blood pressure was measured after a month on each salt, and the change was used to project how many strokes would follow
options.D: Stroke patients and healthy neighbours were asked about their past salt use, and the two groups' answers were compared

items.prompt: How sure is the evidence that eating less sodium lowers blood pressure?

Isometric exercise means holding a muscle still under strain, as in a wall squat or a handgrip squeeze. How sure is the evidence that it lowers blood pressure more than aerobic exercise such as brisk walking or cycling?
In trials where staff supervised diet, weight-loss and exercise programmes, roughly how much did combining several lifestyle changes lower clinic systolic (upper-number) blood pressure?
As a rule of thumb, how much does systolic blood pressure fall for each kilogram of body weight lost?
In large trials where people followed lifestyle programmes in ordinary life, shopping and cooking for themselves, how much further did systolic pressure fall than in a group given advice only?
The same lifestyle programmes lower blood pressure much more in supervised trials than in everyday life. What best explains the gap?

options.A: The body adapts within weeks, so the biological effect of diet and exercise fades
options.B: Supervised trials enrolled people with milder high blood pressure, which responds better
options.C: Everyday studies measured blood pressure less carefully, which hid most of the benefit
options.D: People struggle to sustain the changes when they shop, cook and train on their own

items.prompt: Someone with stage 2 hypertension drinks about one glass of wine a day. What do the trials suggest about cutting it out to lower their blood pressure?

options.A: It should lower systolic pressure by about 5 mmHg, as cutting back does for other drinkers
options.B: Cutting back from two or fewer drinks a day produced no significant fall in blood pressure
options.C: Any reduction in alcohol lowers pressure a little, so it is always worth a few mmHg
options.D: It would raise blood pressure, because light drinking keeps the arteries relaxed

items.prompt: Which reading of the evidence best fits someone newly diagnosed with stage 2 hypertension?

options.A: Lifestyle change still lowers pressure, often more at higher levels, alongside a medical decision on drugs
options.B: Lifestyle change is mainly for mild high blood pressure; at stage 2 its effect is too small to be worth the effort
options.C: Because supervised programmes match a drug's effect, a determined lifestyle overhaul can replace medication
options.D: Lifestyle change only starts to help once drugs have brought pressure down to stage 1 levels

items.prompt: Most lifestyle measures have been shown to lower blood-pressure readings. Which one also has randomised-trial evidence of fewer strokes and deaths?

options.A: Isometric exercise such as wall squats

items.prompt: Which of these questions does the current evidence leave open?

options.A: Whether supervised diet and exercise help people already taking several blood-pressure drugs
options.B: Whether cutting sodium lowers blood pressure more when the starting pressure is higher
options.C: Whether a potassium-enriched salt substitute has been shown to reduce strokes in any population
options.D: Whether combined lifestyle programmes work as well for people starting above 160/100 mmHg
